newsitem.title: INDIA: India children get second dose of polio vaccine.
newsitem.headline: India children get second dose of polio vaccine.

text.p: About 120 million Indian children were vaccinated on Saturday in the second round of an ambitious worldwide campaign to eradicate the crippling disease polio by the year 2000, public health officials said.
Hundreds of thousands of public health workers fanned out across the nation, swarming through homes, airports and railway and bus stations, to complete a task that began last December.
Parents trudged with their children through deep snow to get to the 2,000 health stations in India's northern state of Jammu and Kashmir where the oral vaccine was administered.
Saturday marked the end of the second phase of a three-year programme which began when about 93 million children up to three years of age were innoculated in December 1995 and January 1996.
On December 7 last year, Indian authorities covered 118 million children up to the age of five, out of a targeted 121 million.
"That was the largest such event in world history up to that time," Dr J.K. Andrus, a World Health Organisation (WHO) representative, told Reuters.
On Saturday, the same children received a second dose of vaccine. The two sessions will be repeated a third and last time in late 1997 and early 1998.
"That effort, where every child is immunised, is the one way to flood the community with the vaccine and eradicate the virus," Andrus said.
Initial reports showed the programme was a success, he said.

"But we can only estimate success on the basis of what we have personally seen," Andrus added. "Over the next few days we should be getting reports from all the states, and we expect it to have been a success."

The Indian effort was part of a global drive to wipe out poliomyelitis, an infectious viral disease that strikes the central nervous system and can cause temporary or permanent paralysis. It has already been eradicated in the Americas.
Children are especially vulnerable to the illness, transmitted by human excrement. It thrives in the hot, congested conditions of the Indian subcontinent, according to the WHO.
Health officials said 742 cases of polio had been reported in India in the first nine months of 1996, compared with 2,643 for the same period in 1995.
Since the global eradication drive was launched in 1988, the number of reported cases has fallen by more than 80 percent, to 6,200 from 31,000.
But the WHO estimates that for every documented case, nine go unreported, with two thirds of them in Bangladesh, India and Pakistan.
The polio virus still circulates in some 70 countries.
Recently there have been outbreaks in Chechnya, Pakistan and Zaire, according to Rotary International, which expects to have spent $400 million on the eradication project by 2000.
